A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACECODER. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added content to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model evaluations, reinforcement-learning results and filtering/backbone ablations in Tables 2–6.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original test-case auditing, dataset analysis, RM-Bench evaluations and HumanEval case studies.

M1.justification: The synthesis/filtering pipeline, preference-selection thresholds, Bradley-Terry reward training, scalar reward head and Reinforce++ tuning remain unchanged. The additional prompt and model-role tables provide implementation disclosure without establishing a revised algorithm.

E1.justification: v4 retains HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench and LiveCodeBench and adds RM-Bench evaluations covering Code, Chat, Math and Safety. This substantially extends evaluation beyond coding performance to reward judgments across multiple domains.

E2.justification: The RL comparison replaces its DeepSeek-V2.5 row with RLEF-8B/70B, PPOCoder-7B, StepCoder-7B, CodeGemma-7B and DSTC-33B (v1 Table 3; v4 Table 4). DeepSeek-V2.5 remains elsewhere. The new RM-Bench comparison also includes Nemotron-340B and additional InternLM and Skywork variants.

E3.justification: Core training budgets and generation settings remain unchanged. v4 adds a random audit of 40 questions with five tests each, dataset pass-rate profiling and RM-Bench scoring by domain/difficulty. Table 1 revises the filtered corpus size from 89,422 to 87,149; the PDFs do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filtering, backbone and base-model RL ablations, v4 adds direct human validation of synthesized tests, dataset difficulty analysis in Table 2, and three HumanEval case studies in Appendix A.4. These substantially expand analysis of reliability, successes and failures.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new audit reports raw outcomes and sampling details without uncertainty estimation; generated-candidate counts do not represent repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds RM-Bench averages of 72.2 and 76.1 for the 7B and 32B reward models, three invalid tests among 200 audited tests, dataset pass-rate statistics and comparator/case-study results. Original model scores largely remain unchanged, but summary gains are revised, including the Llama/32B reranking average gain from 10.7 to 9.0.

T1.justification: The Bradley-Terry formulation, PPO ratio/objective, best-of-N selection and preference-selection equation are retained. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and v4 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and central synthesis/reward-training/RL contributions remain. v4 adds an introductory claim of leading RM-Bench performance, including Chat, removes the claim to the first large-scale verifiable code-training dataset, and frames novelty more specifically around combining synthesis with reward-model and RL training.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive limitations concerning incorrect reference solutions, insufficient edge-case coverage and noisy rewards despite passing tests. It also interprets RM-Bench results as generalization beyond coding and explains specific RL regressions and improvements in Appendix A.4. These extend the earlier, narrower reward-hacking discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2/Table 9 explicitly identifies the backbones and preference-generation models for both reward-model sizes. Appendix A.3 adds a reference-program-only synthesis prompt. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware information and access identifiers are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantial positioning against automated test-generation work, including CodeT, Algo and Clover, and expands coding-RL discussion beyond CodeRL to PPOCoder, RLEF, StepCoder and DSTC. The earlier general code-model and reward-model reviews are preserved in Appendix A.1.

P1.justification: The introduction is compressed and refocused, the conclusion and RL-related-work discussion are rewritten, dataset construction becomes a Methodology subsection, and two related-work sections move into the expanded appendix. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative alongside widespread copyediting.

P2.justification: v4 adds four tables covering dataset pass rates, RM-Bench, model roles and another prompt, plus three illustrated code-comparison figures. Existing result tables gain comparator rows, captions move below tables, and table sizing and placement change substantially. Figure 1 is retained.

improvement.justification: The human audit directly examines synthesized-test reliability, while relevant RL comparisons, RM-Bench evaluation, clearer prior-work distinctions and concrete limitations address important validation and positioning gaps in v1. Together these substantially strengthen the paper. The audit remains small and reporting defects persist: v4 Table 8 states a 2.4 gain despite displayed averages of 54.0 and 57.6. These flaws limit some summaries but do not outweigh the broader improvements.
